desc:
A strictly increasing subsequence of nums is obtained by deleting zero or more elements, without reordering the rest, so that the remaining values strictly increase from left to right.

Find the length L of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, then return how many different subsequences have length L. Two subsequences are different if they use different index sets, even when they contain equal values. Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007.
hints: Computing only the length of the longest increasing subsequence is the standard DP: len[i] = 1 + max len[j] over j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].
Along with len[i], keep cnt[i], the number of increasing subsequences of that maximum length that end exactly at index i.

When you scan j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]: if len[j] + 1 beats len[i], set len[i] = len[j] + 1 and cnt[i] = cnt[j]; if it ties, add cnt[j] to cnt[i]. The answer sums cnt[i] over all i with len[i] equal to the global maximum.
editorial: For each index i define len[i], the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at i, and cnt[i], how many subsequences of that length end at i. Initially both are 1 (the element on its own). For every earlier index j with nums[j] < nums[i], the candidate length is len[j] + 1: a strictly larger candidate replaces len[i] and resets cnt[i] = cnt[j], while an equal candidate adds cnt[j] to cnt[i].

Every longest subsequence ends somewhere, so the answer is the sum of cnt[i] over all i whose len[i] equals the maximum length (modulo 1,000,000,007). The double loop is O(n2) time and O(n) space; a Fenwick tree over compressed values can bring it down to O(n log n).
